title: Mendelian Inheritance (Autosomal & Sex-Linked)
objectives: Apply Mendel's laws to pedigree analysis
Differentiate autosomal vs. sex-linked inheritance patterns
Recognize exceptions to classical Mendelian inheritance

autosomal_inheritance.title: Autosomal Patterns
autosomal_inheritance.content:
Dominant Traits
• Affected individuals in every generation
• 50% transmission risk
• Examples: Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome
Recessive Traits
• May skip generations
• 25% risk to offspring of carriers
• Examples: Cystic fibrosis, Sickle cell anemia

sex_linked_inheritance.title: X-Linked Patterns
sex_linked_inheritance.content:
TypeTransmissionMale:Female RatioExample
X-linked RecessiveNo male→male transmissionAffected ♂ > ♀Hemophilia A
X-linked DominantAll daughters of affected ♂ inherit♀ > ♂ (♂ often lethal)Rett syndrome

pedigree_analysis.title: Pedigree Interpretation
pedigree_analysis.content:
Autosomal Dominant Red Flags

Vertical transmission
• Affected parent → 50% affected offspring
• Male-to-male transmission possible
• Example: Neurofibromatosis type 1

X-linked Recessive Clues

Obligate carrier females
• No affected ♀ without affected ♂ in lineage
• Example: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

exceptions.title: Non-Classical Patterns
exceptions.content:
• Incomplete Penetrance: BRCA1 (85% cancer risk by age 70)
  • Variable Expressivity: NF1 café-au-lait vs. plexiform neurofibromas
  • Germline Mosaicism: Recurrence risk >50% for unaffected parents

case_studies.title: Clinical Applications
case_studies.content:
Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

Gene: APC (5q22.2)
Inheritance: Autosomal dominant
Management: Colectomy by age 20-25

Fragile X Syndrome

Gene: FMR1 (Xq27.3)
Mechanism: CGG repeat expansion (>200)
Testing: PCR + Southern blot

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why are X-linked dominant disorders often more severe in males?

Males lack a second X chromosome to compensate (e.g., incontinentia pigmenti is lethal in utero for most males).

How can autosomal recessive conditions appear dominant in pedigrees?

Pseudodominance occurs when a carrier mates with an affected individual (50% affected offspring), common in high-frequency conditions like sickle cell.

Why don't mitochondrial disorders follow X-linked inheritance?

Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited (all children of affected mothers inherit), while X-linked shows specific male-female transmission patterns.
